description.value: The paper reviews sex differences in children's eating behaviors and presents new analyses of sex and weight status in relation to appetitive traits and neural responses to food cues.

spans.text: The purpose of this paper is to critically discuss the literature on sex differences in eating behavior in children and present new findings supporting the role of sex in child appetitive traits and neural responses to food cues.

Post-hoc correlations confirmed a significant positive association between BMI z-score and neural response to higher than lower ED food images in females, while in males this relationship was negative. Although preliminary, these results suggest that increased weight status in female children is positively related to neural engagement to high- relative to low-ED food cues in regions typically associated with contextual processing and visual object recognition, while in male children the opposite pattern was observed.

Food images were presented using MATLAB Version 8 [ 144 ] and viewed through a mirror mounted on the head coil using a magnet-compatible projector.

stimuli.value: A block-design presentation of 180 images: 120 food images, 30 furniture images, and 30 scrambled images. Food images varied by portion size (large or small) and energy density (high-ED or low-ED). High-ED foods included French fries, chicken nuggets, cookies, and pizza; low-ED foods included grilled chicken, carrots, broccoli, and apples.

spans.text: In brief, children viewed a total of 180 images (120 food, 30 furniture, and 30 scrambled images) presented in block design. The food cues differed in portion size (large or small) and energy density (high-ED or low-ED). High-ED foods were >1.5 kcal/gram and included French fries, chicken nuggets, cookies, and pizza. Low-ED foods were <1.5 kcal/gram and included grilled chicken, carrots, broccoli, and apples.
